body:
I only have the problem statement here, plus the fact that a prior node was selected with an empty commitments surface. So I cannot lean on any earlier account of what the flatmates' agreement meant, and I should be explicit that anything I say about that is my own reading, not a recovery of a lost record.

The situation as stated has three interacting features. First, the friends sometimes reach agreement about who will do a chore, but later disagree about what that agreement meant. Second, schedules change, so whatever was agreed may no longer fit the circumstances in which it was made. Third, one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. These are not independent: avoidance makes renegotiation harder, and renegotiation is exactly what shifting schedules would seem to require.

A useful working hypothesis is that the recurring dispute is not mainly about willingness to do chores but about the scope and duration of an agreement. "I'll do the dishes" can mean this once, on my turn, or whenever they pile up; it can mean until schedules change, or until someone says otherwise. If the friends never fixed that, then later disagreement is predictable rather than a sign of bad faith. I do not know from the given material whether this hypothesis is correct; it is a frame for the next conversation, not a finding.

The avoidance matters separately. If one person is staying out of the conversations, pushing harder on the same format is likely to deepen the avoidance. It may help to make the conversation smaller and less accusatory: not "we need to settle the chores" but a short exchange about one recurring friction, at a time when nobody is rushing out. It may also help to put the outcome in writing in a form all three can see, because the disputed meaning is precisely what an unwritten agreement leaves open.

What I would not do is assume that the avoider is the problem. Avoidance often follows from conversations that feel like ambushes, or from being outvoted, or from having given up on being heard. The given material does not tell me which.

A concrete direction: propose a low-stakes review of two or three recurring chores, state each as a scope (what counts as done, over what period, and what happens when schedules change), and ask each person to correct the statement rather than defend a position. If that fails, the more honest question is whether the three of you can agree on a minimal baseline plus a renegotiation trigger, rather than on a fixed division.

I am uncertain about the diagnosis, the appropriate tone, and whether the third friend's avoidance is a symptom or a separate constraint. I also do not know the history of prior attempts, so I cannot claim that any of this is new or that it will work.
commitments: Taking this up would involve treating the scope-and-duration hypothesis as a testable frame rather than a conclusion: the next conversation should try to elicit what each person understood a past agreement to cover, and whether the disagreement is about wording, about changed circumstances, or about something else. It would also involve accepting that the avoidance is a constraint on method, so any attempt to renegotiate has to be designed so that the avoider can participate without being cornered, and dropping the approach if it predictably increases withdrawal. A further commitment is to make the renegotiation trigger explicit, so that a change of schedule does not have to be litigated as a breach. What I am not committing to is the claim that the avoider is acting in bad faith, or that a written roster will resolve the conflict; both would need evidence this material does not provide. If the scope hypothesis turns out to be wrong, the fallback is to look for a different recurring structure in the disputes rather than to press the same frame harder.
